To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the same food odor generates separable responses via the orthonasal and retronasal route.

1) the same odor can elicit distinct responses via different routes of presentation, 2) this is true for food but not non-food odors, and 3) the response is not simply related to the pleasantness of the odor.
The olfactory system is capable of generating separate signals for the same stimulus depending on the route of presentation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of olfactory experience and its relationship to the brain.
the role of olfaction in food perception.
understanding the mechanisms that underlie the ability to identify food odors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
orthonasal and retronasal olfactory perception are two distinct modalities.
the results demonstrate that separability is a function of experience and that separability is dependent upon whether the odor is a food or nonfood.
there are separate signals for orthonasally vs. retronasally perceived food and nonfood odors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are two separate olfactory submodalities that are differentially affected by experience.
the olfactory system is a complex system, and that the way we experience odors depends on the context in which they occur, and the way in which they are presented.
the olfactory system has the ability to process odors based upon the route of stimulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the same food odor may be represented differently depending upon how it is perceived.
the way we experience food odors may be different than the way we experience other types of odors.
the route of odor presentation can be used to generate a separate signal for the same food.
